newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Intel dominates microprocessor market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Intel dominates microprocessor market.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
Technology companies which despair of ever denting Intel's microprocessor monopoly should remember the fate of some recent leaders whose dominance seemed permanent.
International Business Machines sat astride the world of mainframe computers until upstart personal computer companies snatched the business away.
The Soviet Union's seven-decade year hegemony seemed permanent but it crumbled away in what seemed like the blink of an eye.
Britain's seemingly invincible Conservatives fell from grace abruptly earlier this month.
Intel presides over the market for microprocessors, the brains inside personal computers. The hugely profitable Santa Clara, California-based high technology leader towers above its rivals.
But the dynamic, fast moving world of computers can quickly turn on even the most powerful companies. One wrong move and the momentum can turn like an unstoppable tide.
COMPETITION WAITS IN THE WINGS

Young companies like Advanced Micro Devices and Cyrix are waiting in the wings to pounce, while Asian semiconductor firms like NEC Corp and Toshiba Corp of Japan and Samsung Electronics of South Korea are said to be biding their time for market and technical conditions to turn in their favour before making a move.
And this week another challenge appeared, when Digital Equipment Corp announced it planned to sue Intel, alleging patent infringement in Intel's Pentium family of microprocessors.
Digital's suit sought to stop Intel selling its patented technology, and said it wanted "huge" damages.
Intel refrained from immediate comment on the suit.
Later Cyrix filed a separate suit alleging Intel infringed its patents in its Pentium, Pentium Pro and Pentium 2 products.
Intel has ridden the personal computer's wave of popularity, driven by public excitement about the Internet, the world-wide network linked by telephone lines.

U.S. technology research company Dataquest reckons that the market for microprocessors will be worth $33.6 billion by 2000, up from $14.1 billion in 1995. Dataquest says sales this year will rise 27 percent to $19.6 billion.
Analysts believe Intel microprocessors appear in at least 80 percent of the world's PCs; some estimate this as high as 90 percent.

This month, Intel unveiled its latest blockbuster product, the Pentium 2, which the company said helps to process data faster then ever. A flaw was found in the new chip shortly after its launch, but Intel said this was a minor problem.
LENGTHENING PRODUCT CYCLES MIGHT BE KEY FOR RIVALS
So what could possibly stop the sun shining on Intel?
Analysts say a lengthening of the life cycles of PCs from the current two to three years could give new entrants time to gear up to sell microprocessors profitably.
"Useful PC lifecycles will elongate from two to three years to three to five years," said David Vellante, senior vice president of International Data Corporation.

"Longer PC cycles makes it easier for Intel compatible chip vendors to compete, and this could entice Asian producers like NEC, Toshiba and Samsung to aggressively compete, making big investments in capacity or investing in AMD or Cyrix," Vellante said after making a speech here earlier this month.
"Intel's price-cutting tactics could be matched by these deep pocketed Asians," Vellante said.
NEW TECHNOLOGY MIGHT GIVE COMPETITORS A CHANCE
Changes in technology could also upset Intel, according to Dr Alex Beavers, managing partner at Coopers and Lybrand's high technology practice in Boston, Massachusetts.

"The technology is changing and this may be creating new opportunities as well. We are starting to see the system-on-a-chip and this will create further changes in the industry as companies try to position themselves to offer total system capacity on a chip," Beavers said.
Currently, computers come with a microprocessor to provide the brainpower, and provide the link with other components which provide memory and modems to connect with the Internet.
These other components are often supplied by different semiconductor companies.
"In future these different chips will be integrated and printed circuits will get smaller if they exist at all, and could be one large module," Beavers said.
"The industry at large reinvents itself every few years and this volatility gives other companies as well as Intel the chance to reposition to grab new markets," Beavers said.
INTEL LEAD UNASSAILABLE, SAYS ANALYST
But anyone waiting to see Intel stumble is wasting their time, says Jim Eastlake, director of European semiconductor research at Dataquest's British office.
"Intel is in a very strong position. To say that Intel's profits were bigger than the turnover of its nearest rival, starts to sketch the enormity of the difference," Eastlake said.
In 1996, Intel earned net profits of $5.2 billion on sales of $20.8 billion.
Eastlake said that Intel has the ability to quickly supply chips to companies globally.

"Their lead in processing and manufacturing puts them in a position to guarantee sufficient capacity to customers to be able to say if you go to them, you will get the industry standard product in the volume required," Eastlake said.

"Intel is a very together company. It will release five or six new products this year while rivals like AMD and Cyrix will produce one each. It has all the design knowledge in house and all that intellectual property. It has invested in factories which are very costly. You are talking hundreds of billions of dollars to be able to compete with Intel," Eastlake said.
"Over the next four to five years Intel is quite unassailable," Eastlake said.
Other analysts are not so sure.
PRICE SAID TO BE INTEL ACE CARD

Waka Bayashi, senior analyst at Nomura Securities in Tokyo, agrees that Intel has dominated the last 10 years, but wonders if it will be able to do this in the multimedia and video world of the next 10 years.
John Ces, research manager at the Romtec consultancy, questions whether Intel can protect its markets.
"The monopoly has diminished over the last year or so, with COMPAQ designing a PC around the Cyrix chip. I don't think any analyst will say Intel will gain share over the next few years," Ces said.
But Ces says the competition fears above all the price weapon that Intel can bring to bear on upstart competitors.
"If Intel sees its share dropping it could put resources in and blow the competition out of the water," Ces said.
